tabHints.general: Write equations with "=". Use xⁿ for powers, e.g. x^2 is x squared. To plot a function, write y = and then the function.
tabHints.trig: Put the angle in parentheses, e.g. sin(x). Tap π for pi.
tabHints.calculus: Derivative: tap d/dx and type the function inside the parentheses. Second derivative or a derivative at a point: define the function, then use the f′ key to write f''(x) or f'(2). Integral: tap ∫ dx and type the function between ∫ and dx; for a definite integral write the bounds like ∫_0^1.
tabHints.limitLog: Limit: tap lim, type the value x approaches after →, then the function after the parenthesis. Logs: log is base 10, log₂ is base 2.
tabHints.setsVectors: Define each set, separate with commas, then write the question. Write vectors inside [ , ].

arithmetic.title: Arithmetic
arithmetic.summary: Add, subtract, multiply, divide — and the order of operations.
arithmetic.tip: Order of operations: parentheses, then powers, then multiply/divide (left to right), then add/subtract.

fractions.title: Fractions
fractions.summary: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and simplifying fractions.
fractions.tip: To add or subtract, find a common denominator first. To multiply, multiply the numerators and the denominators.

powers.title: Powers
powers.summary: Exponent rules: products, quotients and powers of powers.
powers.tip: With the same base, multiplying adds the exponents, and a power of a power multiplies them.

expressions.title: Simplifying expressions
expressions.summary: Expanding parentheses and combining like terms.
expressions.tip: Only like terms (e.g. 2x and 3x) combine; x terms and constants stay separate.

linear.title: Linear equations
linear.summary: Find the unknown by doing the same thing to both sides.
linear.tip: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other so the equation stays balanced.

quadratic.title: Quadratic equations
quadratic.summary: Solve by factoring or with the quadratic formula.
quadratic.tip: If it factors, set each factor to zero; if not, use the formula and the discriminant (b² - 4ac).

trig.title: Trigonometry
trig.summary: Simplifying sine, cosine and tangent expressions.
trig.tip: Remember the key identity: sin²x + cos²x = 1.

derivative.title: Derivatives
derivative.summary: Term-by-term differentiation with the power rule and trig derivatives.
derivative.tip: Power rule: the derivative of xⁿ is n·xⁿ⁻¹, and the derivative of a constant is 0.

limit.title: Limits
limit.summary: Limits by substitution, resolving 0/0 (factoring or the conjugate), one-sided limits and limits at infinity.
limit.tip: Substitute first. If you get 0/0, factor or multiply by the conjugate; at infinity only the highest powers matter.

logarithm.title: Logarithms & Exponential Equations
logarithm.summary: Logarithmic and exponential equations using the log rules, the definition of a log, and a common base.
logarithm.tip: log(x) is base 10 and ln(x) is base e. Always check the domain: what's inside a log must be positive.

sets.title: Sets
sets.summary: Union, intersection, difference, complement, subsets and the counting formula for a union.
sets.tip: Each element is written once. Key formula: n(A∪B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A∩B).

vectors.title: Vectors & Coordinates
vectors.summary: Adding and subtracting vectors, scalar multiples, the vector between two points and a vector's length.
vectors.tip: Vector AB is B's coordinates minus A's. Add and subtract vectors component by component.

geometry.title: Geometry: area, volume, Pythagoras
geometry.summary: Area and perimeter of shapes, volume and surface area of solids, the Pythagorean theorem and polygon angles.
geometry.tip: The easiest way is the geometry calculator: pick a shape and type the measurements. Answers with π are shown exactly and approximately.

graphs.title: Graphs (discrete math)
graphs.summary: Edges of complete, regular and complement graphs, vertex degrees, and whether a degree sequence is possible.
graphs.tip: The degrees always add up to twice the number of edges (2q), so the sum is even. In a simple graph with p vertices every degree is at most p - 1.

integral.title: Integrals
integral.summary: Indefinite integrals term by term, plus the constant of integration.
integral.tip: Reverse power rule: the integral of xⁿ is xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). Don't forget + C.

typing.title: Typing a problem

items.keys: Symbols your keyboard hides (like √ and powers) are in the key row under the field.
items.digits: Persian digits (۱۲۳) work too — no need to switch keyboards.
items.multiply: No × needed between a number and x: 2x means 2 times x.

typing.tryHint: Tap an example to try it:

rows.power: Power: use ^; x^2 is x squared.
rows.sqrt: Square root: write it inside sqrt( ).
rows.fraction: Fraction: top / bottom; wrap long ones in parentheses.
rows.pi: Pi: pi. Sine and cosine: sin( ) and cos( ).
rows.derivative: Derivative: put the expression inside d/dx( ).
rows.integral: Integral: write the expression between ∫ and dx.
rows.limit: Limit: lim(x→2) then the expression; ∞ for infinity, 0+ or 0- for one-sided limits.
rows.log: Logarithm: log(x) is base 10, log_2(x) base 2, ln(x) base e.
rows.sets: Sets: define them first, e.g. A={1,2,3}, then ask (∪ union, ∩ intersection, - difference, ' complement, n( ) count). Separate parts with commas.
rows.vectors: Vectors: write them in [ , ], e.g. [2, 3]. Points like A(1, 2) and the vector between them AB. Length inside | |.
rows.graphs: Graphs: complete_graph(p=6) edges of K_p, regular_graph(p=8, k=3) a regular graph, complement_edges(p=6, q=9) the complement, degree_sequence(…) does such a graph exist, graph(ab, bc) the vertex degrees.

items.light: Use good light and keep your hand's or phone's shadow off the page.
items.frame: Fit the problem inside the guide frame — not too far, not too close.
items.flat: Hold the phone parallel to the page so the writing isn't skewed.
items.review: If the photo has several problems you'll see a list and can fix each one before solving.

items.steps: Each step shows what it was before, what was done, and the result, with an explanation.

items.verified: The "Verified ✓" badge means the final answer was substituted back and checked.
items.share: Share sends the solution as an image.

items.topics: "Topics" in the menu: explanations, tips and examples per topic.

concepts.meaning: A limit asks what value the function approaches as x gets closer and closer to a — x itself never equals a.
concepts.substitute: Always substitute first. If the function is defined there (polynomials are), the limit is just its value.
concepts.zeroOverZero: Getting 0/0 means an indeterminate form: factor and cancel the common factor, or multiply by the conjugate when there is a root.
concepts.infinite: A nonzero number over 0 means the function blows up. Check the left and right limits; if they differ, the limit does not exist.
concepts.atInfinity: As x goes to infinity, only the highest-power terms of a polynomial fraction matter.

steps.factor1: Substituting gives an indeterminate form, so simplify first.
steps.factor3: Cancel the common factor — allowed because x approaches 2 but never equals it.
steps.conjugate2: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the numerator to clear the root.

mistakes.zeroOverZero: Treating 0/0 as 0 or 1. It is not an answer — it tells you to simplify.
mistakes.infinityOverInfinity: Infinity over infinity is indeterminate too and need not be 1 — compare the highest powers.
mistakes.sides: Not checking both sides when the denominator becomes 0. Here the right limit is +∞ and the left −∞, so the limit does not exist.

concepts.meaning: A logarithm answers "which power?": log base b of A is c exactly when b to the power c is A.
concepts.bases: log with no base means base 10; ln means base e.
concepts.product: The log of a product is the sum of the logs.
concepts.quotient: The log of a quotient is the difference of the logs.
concepts.power: A power inside a log comes out in front.
concepts.domain: What is inside a log must be positive. Write the domain first and check your answers against it at the end.
concepts.exponential: For an exponential equation, write both sides with the same base and equate the exponents; if that is impossible, take a log of both sides.

examples.sameBase: An exponential equation with a common base

steps.logEquation2: Combine the two logs into one.
steps.logEquation3: Rewrite as a power, by the definition of a log.
steps.logEquation5: Reject the answer that breaks the domain.
steps.sameBase1: Write both sides as powers of 3.

mistakes.sum: Splitting the log of a sum. That rule only holds for a product.
mistakes.domain: Not checking the domain and keeping an answer that makes a log argument zero or negative.
mistakes.quotient: Confusing a quotient of logs with the log of a quotient.

concepts.meaning: A set is a collection of distinct objects: each element is written once and order does not matter.
concepts.union: Union: every element that is in at least one of the sets.
concepts.intersection: Intersection: only the elements in both sets.
concepts.difference: A minus B: the elements of A that are not in B. Order matters.
concepts.complement: Complement of A: the elements of the universal set U that are not in A.
concepts.subsets: A set with n elements has 2 to the n subsets, counting the empty set and the set itself.
concepts.counting: To count a union, subtract the shared elements once, since they were counted twice.

steps.operations3: Remove the intersection from the union.
steps.counting2: Substitute the numbers and call the unknown x.

mistakes.repeat: Writing a shared element twice in a union.
mistakes.order: Treating A minus B and B minus A as the same.
mistakes.counting: Adding the counts without subtracting the intersection — shared elements get counted twice.

concepts.meaning: A vector is a directed segment with a size and a direction. The first component is the horizontal move, the second the vertical move.
concepts.fromPoints: The vector from A to B is B's coordinates minus A's (end minus start).
concepts.add: Add and subtract vectors component by component.
concepts.scale: Multiplying by a number multiplies every component; a negative number reverses the direction.
concepts.length: A vector’s length comes from Pythagoras.

examples.length: Length of the vector between two points

mistakes.direction: Start minus end — the vector points the wrong way.
mistakes.length: Taking the sum of the components as the length.

concepts.areaPerimeter: Area is how much surface a shape covers (square units); perimeter is the distance around it (length units).
concepts.circle: Area and circumference of a circle, with π.
concepts.pythagoras: Pythagoras holds only in a right triangle: the square of the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two.
concepts.prism: Prism and cylinder volume: base area times height. A pyramid or cone is one third of that.
concepts.sphere: Volume and surface area of a sphere.
concepts.polygon: Sum of the interior angles of an n-gon, in degrees. The exterior angles always add up to 360°.

steps.pythagoras1: The hypotenuse is known, so the missing side is hypotenuse squared minus the other side squared.
steps.pythagoras3: Take the square root; a length is positive.

mistakes.hypotenuse: Adding the squares when the hypotenuse is the known side.
mistakes.diameter: Using the diameter instead of the radius; the radius is half the diameter.
mistakes.third: Forgetting to divide by 3 for a pyramid or cone.

concepts.meaning: A graph is made of vertices and edges: p is the number of vertices (order), q the number of edges (size). A simple graph has no loops or multiple edges.
concepts.degree: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges at it. In a simple graph with p vertices, a degree is at most p − 1.
concepts.handshake: The degrees add up to twice the number of edges, because each edge has two ends — so there is always an even number of odd-degree vertices.
concepts.complete: In a complete graph every two vertices are joined.
concepts.regular: In a k-regular graph every vertex has degree k.
concepts.complement: The complement has the same vertices and exactly the edges the graph does not have.

examples.regular: Is there a 3-regular graph on 7 vertices?

steps.regular2: The degree sum is odd but must be even, so no such graph exists.
steps.sequence1: The degree sum is even — the necessary condition holds.
steps.sequence2: Havel–Hakimi: remove the largest degree and subtract 1 from that many of the next degrees.
steps.sequence3: Repeat until everything is 0 — so the graph exists.

mistakes.evenOnly: Thinking an even degree sum is enough. This sum is even, yet no simple graph has these degrees.
mistakes.complete: Counting each edge of a complete graph twice — divide by 2.
mistakes.maxDegree: A degree equal to or larger than the number of vertices in a simple graph.
